title: Mamdani Joins Hindu Festivities in Queens, Urges Unity After Illinois Temple Plot
excerpt: New York's mayor danced garba and performed aarti during Navratri celebrations, tying the festivities to solidarity after the attempted shooting at the Aurora Balaji temple.
body:
• New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined Hindu New Yorkers in Queens for Navratri, Durga Puja, Dashain and Vijayadashami celebrations.
  • He linked the festivities to solidarity after last week's attempted mass shooting at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) temple in Aurora, Illinois.
  • In Congress, 105 lawmakers led by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi have asked the FBI to investigate the Aurora attempt as a potential federal hate crime.
  • Prosecutors say the 19-year-old suspect's rifle jammed outside the temple and a coworker alerted police before he could return.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined Hindu New Yorkers in Queens this week to celebrate Navratri, Durga Puja, Dashain and Vijayadashami, using the festivities to call for unity against hate after the attempted mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois.

"This week, I was blessed to join Hindu New Yorkers in Queens celebrating Navratri, Durga Puja, Dashain, and Vijayadashami. We danced garba, performed aarti, witnessed Sindoor Khela, and honored the Goddess Durga," Mamdani said in a post on X on Wednesday, reported by India Today.

"May we all join together in our shared responsibility to stand against hate and care for one another. Jai Mata Ki."

— Zohran Mamdani, Mayor of New York City

The Aurora plot behind the message

Mamdani said it was an honour to celebrate "especially after the attempted mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois last week." The reference was to the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) temple in Aurora, where prosecutors say 19-year-old Alexandros Paporakis attempted to shoot a man outside the temple on October 11, the first day of Navratri, but his rifle jammed. He allegedly spoke of returning, a coworker alerted police, and he was arrested.

https://x.com/NYCMayor/status/2113034746288636235

The response in Washington has widened this week. Illinois Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, who was worshipping at the temple with his family when the incident occurred, led 105 members of Congress in urging FBI Director Kash Patel to investigate the attempt as a potential federal hate crime. Leaders of the Democratic National Committee's Asian American and Pacific Islander Caucus and Interfaith Council have also condemned the alleged plot, framing it as an attack on religious freedom itself.

Why the Queens visit carries weight

Navratri ran from October 11 to October 19 this year, with Vijayadashami on October 20. Queens is home to one of the largest Hindu communities in the United States, and mayoral visits to its temples during the festival season are a fixture of New York politics. Mamdani, the city's first Muslim and Indian American mayor, has made interfaith visibility a theme of his tenure; his mother, filmmaker Mira Nair, was raised Hindu, a background he has spoken about publicly.

For Hindu American organisations, the sequence matters: a foiled attack on a temple during Navratri, a congressional push for a federal hate-crime investigation, and now the mayor of the country's largest city celebrating the same festival in public and naming the attack. Community leaders have argued that plots like Aurora's grow out of a surge in anti-Hindu rhetoric online, and that visible solidarity from elected officials is part of the deterrent.

The Aurora case now moves through the courts, with the suspect's next hearing due at the end of October, while the FBI decides whether to open the hate-crime investigation lawmakers have requested.
